https://www.theguardian.com/world/video/.text: Italy Ancient Roman pottery discovered in shipwreck off Sicilian coast – video Italy's Carabinieri cultural protection unit has discovered the wreck of a Roman ship off Sicily. Divers found hundreds of amphorae and parts of anchors inside the vessel, which was located about 3 miles off the coast of Mazara del Vallo. https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text: The survival of the chicken liver sponge in the harsh environment of a Spanish harbour suggests it could be used to help clean up pollution in ports. Photograph: Carlota Escarré View image in fullscreen The survival of the chicken liver sponge in the harsh environment of a Spanish harbour suggests it could be used to help clean up pollution in ports. Photograph: Carlota Escarré Seascape: the state of our oceans Marine life Could this humble sea sponge clean up the world’s ports? The chicken liver sponge has sailed through a test of its ability to filter pollutants in a harbour in Spain’s Costa Brava Seascape: the state of our oceans is supported by About this content Sara Hashemi Tue 1 Sep 2026 04.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google In the polluted waters of Marina Palamós on Spain’s Costa Brava, Manuel Maldonado, a sponge biologist, noticed something unusual last month: red starfish had started settling in the area. Nearly two years earlier, the Spanish National Research Council scientist and his colleagues had begun transplanting sea sponges into the port to study whether they could survive in its polluted waters. Only one species, the chicken liver sponge ( Chondrosia reniformis , also called the kidney sponge), which is found along the Mediterranean coast but rarely seen in the harbour, managed to survive. Its resilience, and the arrival of the red starfish, suggests sponges could be used to clean up pollution in ports. View image in fullscreen Researchers monitored the sponges’ health using underwater photography and close inspection. Photograph: Carlota Escarré Sea sponges are some of the Earth’s oldest ecosystem engineers. Previous research has shown that abundant communities can reshape their surroundings in positive ways. They can filter pollutants from enormous volumes of water, cycling nutrients in the process. They also enhance biodiversity by attracting marine animals that live within and around them, such as worms and crustaceans. All of this points to their potential as a tool for renaturalising harbours, some of the most disturbed marine environments in the world. The accumulation of pollutants such as rubbish and oil, the introduction of invasive species from ships and persistent noise pollution make it incredibly difficult for marine life to thrive there. But first, it has to be proved that sponges can survive in harsh environments. “So we tested different Spanish species with the idea of finding some that could survive in a harbour environment,” says Maldonado, who led the research. The team focused on five sponge species commonly found on the coast, chosen because their abundance suggests they are good survivors. “You also don’t want to use a very sensitive or protected species,” he says. “It has to be something you can handle and transport to the harbour.” The sponges were collected from a site about 18 miles (30km) south of the harbour where they were transplanted. Maldonado’s student and study co-author, Carlota Escarré, monitored their health using underwater photography and inspection. Escarré conducted dives every 20 to 64 days over the course of 15 months, braving early hours and cold waters at the harbour. View image in fullscreen Regular dives to examine the sponges were conducted over 15 months. Photograph: Per Manuel All the red encrusting sponges ( Crambe crambe ) , leather sponges ( Scalarispongia scalaris ) and stinker sponges ( Ircinia oros ) shrank and eventually died during the study. But almost 92% of the chicken liver sponge specimens survived the polluted water. “It was a surprise for all of us,” says Escarré. Some even managed to reproduce asexually, bringing their numbers up to 40 from 24. Experts hope the study finally puts sea sponges, long overlooked in favour of the more charismatic coral, on the map. “This study shows what we in the sea sponge community have known for years,” says Andreu Santín Muriel, a marine biologist at the University of Porto’s Interdisciplinary Centre of Marine and Environmental Research, who was not involved in the work. “Sponges are excellent potential species for bioremediation and habitat recovery.” He adds: “A lot of effort has been put in the past decades for coral restoration; we understand the importance of corals very well. But sponges provide more ecosystem services, yet they’re not as attractive, so they have received way less money.” David Amptmeijer, a doctoral researcher at Helmholtz-Zentrum Hereon, who was not involved in the research, says it is important to note how localised the study is. It is unclear if these same sponges could survive, for example, in a harbour in Maine. View image in fullscreen Researchers will keep monitoring the sponges over several years. Photograph: Carlota Escarré Though Amptmeijer believes sea sponges have great potential for pollution management, he says a lot more research is needed before scientists can fully understand how they interact with pollutants. Maldonado suspects the chicken liver sponge – a high-microbial-abundance sponge (hosting diverse communities of symbiotic microorganisms within its tissues) that takes ammonium from seawater and releases nitrate – is able to cope with pollution thanks to its diverse microbiome. “We will start working on this after the summer,” he says. He and his team will continue monitoring the sponges over several years, but they also hope to study other organisms: he has written a proposal for a project that combines sponges with oysters, which are also powerful filter feeders. Santín Muriel says sponges have been around for at least 600m years. “They have survived at least five mass extinctions, and they’re still thriving in today’s oceans. That means they’ve most likely already encountered a lot of environmental problems throughout their existence.” It’s not so strange, then, to think that sea sponges may already have the solutions to many of the problems humans face today. “We tend to look more to technology to solve environmental pollution,” Santín Muriel says. “But marine organisms most likely have already developed toolkits that could help us clean the oceans.” Explore more on these topics Marine life Seascape: the state of our oceans Oceans Pollution Animals Wildlife Spain Europe features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution Green light

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: A participant displays a placard with the lettering 'No AfD' in front of the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin on 7 September 2026. Photograph: John MacDougall/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A participant displays a placard with the lettering 'No AfD' in front of the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin on 7 September 2026. Photograph: John MacDougall/AFP/Getty Images Opinion One Nation The far right is becoming normalised in Germany – and winning. Australia should take heed Charlotte Feakins One Nation and the AfD may not look the same, but they are singing from the same song sheet - and both have had recent electoral success Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Sat 12 Sep 2026 16.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 12 Sep 2026 19.59 EDT Share The recent win for the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in Germany is shocking, except it’s not shocking. The writing has been on the wall for quite some time. Last Sunday, the far-right, pro-Russian and anti-immigration AfD won almost 44% of the vote in the election in Saxony-Anhalt, a largely rural state in the former East Germany, more than doubling its previous result and finishing far ahead of the Christian Democrats. Why is the far-right AfD’s state victory significant and what might happen next in German politics? Read more It sits within a troubling global trend. In 2025, nearly one in four countries worldwide experienced democratic backsliding , with Europe and North America home to six of the 10 countries newly identified as autocratising, including Italy, the UK and the US. Despite the cultural and historical differences, Australia is not immune. We cannot afford to be complacent. This time last year, I travelled to Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, a predominantly rural region in Germany’s north-east, to examine the culture of the far right and its counter-responses as part of my research. Like Saxony-Anhalt, it’s an area where the AfD has significant support. My colleagues and I spent days walking the streets of towns and cities, including Rostock and Greifswald, as well as attending an anti-fascist music festival. We wanted to understand how extremism was encountered and expressed in everyday life. But what we found, or more precisely did not find, surprised us. View image in fullscreen ‘Antifa’ graffiti in Rostock, Germany, 2025. Photograph: Charlotte Feakins For a politics so extreme and increasingly popular, visual expressions of the far right were remarkably scarce. We encountered graffitied walls and hundreds of activist stickers on street signs, lamp-posts and electricity boxes. Of these, only one or two were associated with the far right. The counter-movement dominated the streetscape. Its stickers and graffiti were vibrant, loud and sharp, with a clear intent and recurring “anti-fascist” message. Yet a subtler pattern was emerging. The far right was made visible not through its own stickers or graffiti, but in the intolerance directed towards the counter-movement: freshly placed anti-fascist and pro-refugee stickers were being actively defaced. View image in fullscreen A ‘Refugees Welcome’ sticker defaced, Greifswald, Germany, 2025. Photograph: Charlotte Feakins Looking back now, that landscape feels strangely prescient. As far-right ideas move beyond the fringe and enter mainstream political discourse, they become harder to detect, let alone recognise as extreme – an insidious process that gradually reshapes what is considered “normal”. In Australia, we tend to imagine the far right as young white men dressed in black and wearing balaclavas, marching through the streets, performing Nazi salutes or standing in front of historic buildings holding banners. These deliberate acts of spectacle are designed to attract attention, provoke and intimidate. They are easy to identify and condemn, appearing separate from the political mainstream. But far-right politics does not only appear wearing a balaclava. Increasingly, it does not look extreme at all. Across Europe, far-right politicians are neat, polished and smooth-talking. They are unnervingly normal . Their messages are often simple and repeatable, circulating like memes through algorithm-driven news feeds, amplified by increasingly powerful actors in the tech and media sectors and, in some cases, legitimised at the ballot box. While One Nation politicians are a long way from the smooth-talking politicians we see in the AfD, the minor party’s recent successes in byelections in Farrer and Secret Harbour should make us take notice. View image in fullscreen AfD’s Tino Chrupalla (L), Ulrich Siegmund and Alice Weidel. ‘At a time when the future feels increasingly uncertain, far-right politics offers something simple and seductive: certainty, belonging and the promise of a return to an imagined past.’ Photograph: Maja Hitij/Getty Images AfD and One Nation may not look or even sound the same, but they are singing from the same song sheet. Their histories, politics and contexts are different, but both draw on exclusion, national restoration, grievance and distrust. Their growing electoral success raises a critical question: why are these ideas finding a more receptive audience now? Across the world authoritarians want to tell us what a ‘good life’ looks like. Here’s how liberals must respond | Alexandre Lefebvre Read more Part of the answer may lie in how the future is imagined. Climate disruption is intensifying amid economic insecurity, war and displacement. AI is transforming how we work, communicate and understand what is real, while immense wealth and technological power are increasingly concentrated in the hands of a few. These are real, present-day challenges, and the anxiety surrounding them is being amplified through social media feeds in which extreme, frightening and divisive versions of events can dominate. At a time when the future feels increasingly uncertain, rightwing populist politics offers something simple and seductive: certainty, belonging and the promise of a return to an imagined past. As these pressures compound, their impacts radiate through our economies, communities and politics. Instead of looking sideways for someone to blame, we need to think more critically: to question where power is held, who benefits from the decisions being made, and who is being asked to bear their consequences. Otherwise, legitimate fears about the future can too easily be used to turn people against each other.
